A point at which pending changes are flushed to disk so recovery need not replay the whole log.
explanation: A checkpoint: A point at which pending changes are flushed to disk so recovery need not replay the whole log.

prompt:
Which term matches this description?

A transaction takes the database from one valid state to another, keeping every constraint true.
explanation: Consistency: A transaction takes the database from one valid state to another, keeping every constraint true.

prompt:
Which term matches this description?

Two transactions read the same value and both write it back, so one change overwrites the other.
explanation: A lost update: Two transactions read the same value and both write it back, so one change overwrites the other.

prompt:
Which term matches this description?

A marker inside a transaction that later statements can be rolled back to without undoing the whole transaction.
explanation: A SAVEPOINT: A marker inside a transaction that later statements can be rolled back to without undoing the whole transaction.

prompt:
Which term matches this description?

Re-running a query in one transaction and getting extra or missing rows because another transaction inserted or deleted them.
explanation: A phantom read: Re-running a query in one transaction and getting extra or missing rows because another transaction inserted or deleted them.

prompt:
Which term matches this description?

Reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values because another transaction committed a change in between.
explanation: A non-repeatable read: Reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values because another transaction committed a change in between.

prompt: Which statement best describes OLAP?
options: An index that determines the physical order of the rows; a table can have only one.
An index built on several columns, useful when queries filter on its leading columns.
Workloads of large analytical queries over historical data.
An index with one entry for every record.
explanation: OLAP: Workloads of large analytical queries over historical data.

prompt: Which statement best describes OLTP?
options: Workloads of many short read-write transactions, such as placing orders.
An index that finds exact matches quickly but cannot answer range queries.
A separate structure that points to the rows without changing their physical order.
A balanced tree whose leaves hold all the keys in sorted order and are linked for range scans.
explanation: OLTP: Workloads of many short read-write transactions, such as placing orders.

prompt: Which statement best describes a B+ tree?
options: An index with one entry for every record.
Workloads of many short read-write transactions, such as placing orders.
A balanced tree whose leaves hold all the keys in sorted order and are linked for range scans.
An index with one entry per block, pointing to the first record in it.
explanation: A B+ tree: A balanced tree whose leaves hold all the keys in sorted order and are linked for range scans.

prompt: Which statement best describes a hash index?
options: Workloads of many short read-write transactions, such as placing orders.
An index with one entry for every record.
An index with one entry per block, pointing to the first record in it.
An index that finds exact matches quickly but cannot answer range queries.
explanation: A hash index: An index that finds exact matches quickly but cannot answer range queries.

prompt: Which statement best describes a dense index?
options: An index that determines the physical order of the rows; a table can have only one.
An index that finds exact matches quickly but cannot answer range queries.
A balanced tree whose leaves hold all the keys in sorted order and are linked for range scans.
An index with one entry for every record.
explanation: A dense index: An index with one entry for every record.

prompt: Which statement best describes a sparse index?
options: A balanced tree whose leaves hold all the keys in sorted order and are linked for range scans.
An index that determines the physical order of the rows; a table can have only one.
Workloads of large analytical queries over historical data.
An index with one entry per block, pointing to the first record in it.
explanation: A sparse index: An index with one entry per block, pointing to the first record in it.

prompt: Which statement best describes a covering index?
options: A balanced tree whose leaves hold all the keys in sorted order and are linked for range scans.
An index with one entry per block, pointing to the first record in it.
An index with one entry for every record.
An index that contains every column a query needs, so the table itself is never read.
explanation: A covering index: An index that contains every column a query needs, so the table itself is never read.

prompt: Which statement best describes a clustered index?
options: A balanced tree whose leaves hold all the keys in sorted order and are linked for range scans.
An index that determines the physical order of the rows; a table can have only one.
An index that finds exact matches quickly but cannot answer range queries.
Workloads of large analytical queries over historical data.
explanation: A clustered index: An index that determines the physical order of the rows; a table can have only one.

prompt: Which statement best describes a composite index?
options: Workloads of large analytical queries over historical data.
An index built on several columns, useful when queries filter on its leading columns.
An index that contains every column a query needs, so the table itself is never read.
An index with one entry for every record.
explanation: A composite index: An index built on several columns, useful when queries filter on its leading columns.

prompt: Which statement best describes a non-clustered index?
options: An index that finds exact matches quickly but cannot answer range queries.
Workloads of large analytical queries over historical data.
A separate structure that points to the rows without changing their physical order.
An index that determines the physical order of the rows; a table can have only one.
explanation: A non-clustered index: A separate structure that points to the rows without changing their physical order.

prompt: A hash table has 7 slots (0 to 6) and uses h(k) = k mod 7. Which slot does key 13 hash to?
explanation: h(k) = k mod m gives the home slot. With linear probing a key whose home slot is taken moves to the next free slot, wrapping round at the end. With chaining, keys that share a slot are kept in a list at that slot.
